125 Airport Road ■ Concord, NH 03301-7300 ■ 603.225.0900 ■ Fax: 603.225.4346 ■ http://www.nhha.org 
 
June 15, 2026 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
Re: CMS-0062-P; Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care 
Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified 
Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges 
 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
On behalf of the New Hampshire Hospital Association (NHHA), we appreciate the opportunity to 
comment on CMS’ proposed rule to improve interoperability and streamline prior authorization 
for drugs. NHHA strongly supports policies that reduce administrative burden, enhance patient 
access to medically necessary care and create more transparent, predictable payor processes. 
We appreciate CMS’ continued work to build on the 2020 interoperability framework and the 
2024 prior authorization final rule by extending many of those requirements to drugs and 
proposing updated standards for the electronic exchange of prior authorization information. 
New Hampshire’s hospitals and health systems experience the effects of fragmented prior 
authorization processes every day. Delays in approvals for physician-administered drugs, 
infusion therapies, oncology treatments, specialty pharmaceuticals and other medically 
necessary services can postpone care, increase staffing burdens, create confusion for patients 
and contribute to avoidable utilization elsewhere in the system. For that reason, we welcome 
proposals that would expand electronic prior authorization for drugs, improve denial 
communications, align decision timeframes more closely across programs and increase public 
accountability for payor prior authorization practices. 
Overall, NHHA appreciates CMS’ effort to modernize prior authorization for drugs, improve 
transparency and strengthen interoperability across the health care system. If finalized and 
effectively implemented, many of these proposals could reduce provider burden and help 
patients receive medically necessary drugs more quickly. We urge CMS to finalize these 
 
provisions with strong standards for denial specificity, practical usability and meaningful 
accountability for payor performance.  
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule and for your consideration of 
our perspective. Our detailed comments are attached. If you have questions or would like 
additional information, please contact Christian Ramsey, Director of Financial Policy & 
Reimbursement, by phone at 603-415-4253 or by email at cramsey@nhha.org. 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Steve Ahnen 
President 
New Hampshire Hospital Association 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
BACKGROUND 
 
Prior authorization is commonly described by health plans as a utilization management 
tool intended to ensure that patients receive coverage for care that is medically 
appropriate and evidence based. In concept, NHHA recognizes that prior 
authorization serves a role in supporting appropriate coverage determinations. In 
practice, however, prior authorization is frequently implemented in ways that delay care, 
disrupt treatment and impose substantial administrative burden on clinicians and care 
teams. 
Impact of Prior Authorization on Provider Burden and Patient Care 
 
The consequences of these processes extend beyond administrative inefficiency. 
Providers consistently report that prior authorization delays can postpone diagnoses, 
interrupt ongoing treatment regimens and create uncertainty for patients and care teams 
alike. These challenges are exacerbated by inconsistent payor requirements, limited 
transparency into coverage criteria and a lack of standardized electronic workflows. The 
resulting delays and disruptions to care are particularly concerning for patients with 
serious, complex or time-sensitive medical needs. 
 
Survey data reinforce these experiences. In a national survey of practicing physicians 
conducted by the American Medical Association, 95% of physicians reported that prior 
authorization delays access to necessary care, and 79% reported that prior 
authorization can at least sometimes lead to patients abandoning their recommended 
course of treatment.1 In addition, about 1 in 4 physicians reported that prior 
authorization led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care, including 
hospitalization, a life-threatening event or the need for intervention to prevent 
permanent impairment or damage.2 These findings underscore that inefficiencies in 
prior authorization processes are not solely administrative in nature but also can have 
significant negative consequences for patients’ health. 
 
Prior authorization also places a heavy burden on clinicians and the health care 
workforce. Physicians and their staff complete, on average, approximately 40 prior 
authorization requests per physician per week, spending nearly two business days each 
week on prior authorization-related activities.3 Moreover, most hospitals have teams of 
 
1 https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf 
2 Ibid. 
3 Ibid. 
 
staff dedicated exclusively to managing prior authorization requirements, and the vast 
majority of physicians describe the burden associated with prior authorization as high or 
extremely high.4 5 These administrative demands divert time and resources away from 
direct patient care and contribute to workforce burnout. 
 
Interoperability as a Foundation for Electronic Prior Authorization 
 
A central driver of these burdens is the absence of consistent interoperability across 
payors, providers and health IT systems. Providers must navigate a patchwork of 
submission methods, documentation requirements and timelines, many of which 
continue to rely on manual processes such as phone calls or proprietary payor portals. 
Even when electronic options are available, they are frequently payor-specific and 
poorly integrated into clinical workflows, requiring duplicative data entry and repeated 
follow-up that erodes potential efficiencies and increases the likelihood of errors, denials 
and rework that drive delays and disruptions in needed patient care. 
 
CMS took an important step with the 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final 
rule, which established new requirements to modernize and streamline prior 
authorization processes for non-drug items and services. Because the rule did not 
extend to drugs, including those covered under a patient’s medical benefit, it left a gap 
in the administrative simplification framework. NHHA therefore applauds CMS’ 
proposal to extend interoperability and prior authorization requirements to these 
drug therapies. 
 
NHHA is particularly focused on the implications for drugs covered under the medical 
benefit, including chemotherapy, immunotherapy, biologics and other 
provider-administered therapies. These treatments are often used to manage serious, 
complex and life-threatening conditions and are commonly furnished in hospital 
outpatient departments, infusion centers and other provider-based settings. For these 
patients, timely access and continuity of care are critical; delays in authorization or 
mid-treatment disruptions can compromise clinical outcomes, exacerbate patient 
distress and undermine carefully coordinated care plans. Providers continue to report 
significant challenges in obtaining prior authorization for these therapies, including 
repeated documentation requests, unclear coverage criteria and limited transparency 
into authorization status.6 These inefficiencies contribute to delays in the initiation and 
 
4 Ibid. 
5 Examples provided by AHA member hospitals 
6 https://oig.hhs.gov/documents/evaluation/3150/OEI-09-18-00260-Complete%20Report.pdf 
 
continuation of care and increase the administrative burden for providers. 
 
These persistent challenges highlight the need for increased efficiency, and the 
proposed rule’s interoperability provisions could meaningfully improve prior 
authorization processes. Standardized electronic exchange can reduce the 
administrative resources spent identifying, assembling, transmitting and re-transmitting clinical 
information across multiple systems and payor workflows. However, these 
policies will only be effective if they are implemented in such a way that aligns with 
clinical workflows and requires payors to clearly identify, accept, and act upon the 
information needed to support a prior authorization request. When interoperability is 
designed thoughtfully, these requirements could reduce the resources that providers 
spend compiling, submitting, and resubmitting documentation across multiple payor 
portals and processes, promote more complete submissions at the outset of the 
request and support more timely payor determinations. 
 
NHHA appreciates CMS’ continued emphasis on interoperability as a 
foundational component of administrative simplification and recognizes the 
coordinated approach reflected in this proposal with the ONC. Interoperability serves as 
the underlying infrastructure that enables electronic prior authorization to function 
effectively at scale, supporting consistent information exchange and alignment across 
payors, providers, technology developers and other stakeholders. Establishing and 
maintaining this foundation is essential to moving from fragmented, manual processes 
toward a more reliable and sustainable electronic prior authorization process that 
supports patient access and care delivery 
ELECTRONIC PRIOR AUTHORIZATION FOR DRUGS 
NHHA supports CMS’ proposal to require impacted payors to support electronic prior 
authorization for drugs and to extend existing prior authorization API requirements to drugs 
covered under a medical benefit. We also support requiring standards that allow more 
automated exchanges of prior authorization information for pharmacy benefits. These changes 
should reduce reliance on manual portals, faxes, phone calls and duplicative documentation 
requests that take clinical staff away from patient care. From the hospital perspective, a more 
consistent electronic prior authorization process across drug benefits is especially important 
because the site of care, benefit design and clinical pathway for many therapies are complex 
and often time sensitive. 
 
 
 
REQUIREMENT TO INCLUDE SPECIFIC DENIAL REASON 
NHHA strongly supports CMS’ proposal to require payors to provide a specific reason for denial 
when a prior authorization request for a drug is not approved. This is an important transparency 
protection. Too often, providers receive vague denial messages that do not identify the 
applicable coverage criteria, missing documentation or clinical reason for the adverse 
determination. Generic statements such as “not medically necessary” do not allow hospitals or 
prescribing clinicians to respond efficiently, correct deficiencies or advise patients accurately. 
We urge CMS to adopt a stronger specificity standard, so denial notices clearly identify the 
basis for the decision, the documentation or clinical information missing from the submission 
and the steps needed for resubmission or appeal. 
IMPROVING COMMUNICATIONS AND DECISION TIMEFRAMES FOR PRIOR AUTHORIZATIONS 
NHHA appreciates CMS’ effort to align and shorten decision timeframes for prior authorization 
requests involving drugs. Timely determinations are essential for hospital departments that 
often coordinate care on tight timelines. We support proposals that would create more 
consistent response expectations across payors and drug types because variation in payor 
timelines is itself an administrative burden. At the same time, we urge CMS to keep exploring 
ways in future rulemaking to shorten turnaround times for clinically urgent therapies and for 
ongoing treatment when patients have already shown stability on a regimen. Repeated prior 
authorization requirements for longstanding drugs can be especially burdensome and may 
interrupt care without improving clinical oversight. 
PRIOR AUTHORIZATION METRICS 
NHHA supports CMS’ proposal to require public reporting of prior authorization metrics for 
drugs and to expand reporting to include numeric counts rather than percentages alone. More 
complete reporting can help show whether a payor’s prior authorization practices are creating 
unnecessary barriers to care and can help employers, purchasers, regulators, providers and 
patients better understand plan behavior. We encourage CMS to ensure that publicly reported 
metrics are easy to find, use consistent definitions across programs and distinguish standard 
and expedited requests, initial denials, approvals after appeal and approvals or denials 
following extended review.  
NHHA also encourages CMS to improve the usefulness of these metrics by requiring more 
granular reporting wherever feasible. Aggregate reporting can obscure where delays and denials 
occur and limit the value of the data for patients, providers and regulators. We encourage CMS 
to move toward service-level or drug-level reporting, require plans to post this information in 
a standardized and easy-to-find location on their websites and consider hosting the data on a 
centralized CMS platform so it can be reviewed and compared more easily. 
 
UPDATED INTEROPERABILITY STANDARDS, IMPLEMENTATION GUIDES AND API REPORTING 
NHHA appreciates CMS and HHS’s continued emphasis on updated FHIR-based standards, 
implementation guides and reporting of interoperability API endpoints and usage metrics. 
Consistent technical requirements are important to reduce custom interfaces and help 
hospitals, clinicians, EHR vendors and payors move toward more scalable exchange. However, 
implementation success will depend heavily on real-world usability. Our members remain 
concerned that, without strong operational expectations and testing, payors may technically 
comply while still maintaining burdensome workflows, inconsistent documentation 
requirements or incomplete data exchange. We therefore encourage CMS to pair technical 
standards with ongoing oversight of API functionality, reliability and practical usability from 
the provider perspective. 
NHHA also urges CMS to distinguish between technical conformance and operational usability 
when evaluating payor compliance. APIs that technically meet a standard but fail to return 
actionable information, fit into clinical workflows or reduce reliance on manual workarounds 
will not achieve the rule’s goals. We encourage CMS to require robust conformance testing, 
transparency into testing results and clear fallback expectations when electronic prior 
authorization transactions fail so hospitals are not pushed back into fragmented manual 
processes. 
NHHA also supports CMS’ proposal to require impacted payors to report and publish 
interoperability API endpoints and related technical information. Hospitals’ ability to use 
electronic prior authorization, retrieve coverage information and connect to required APIs 
depends on timely, accurate and standardized endpoint information. Without a centralized and 
authoritative mechanism for identifying payor endpoints, hospitals and vendors must rely on 
fragmented, manual processes that undercut the efficiency these policies are meant to create. 
We encourage CMS to ensure that endpoint information is published in a consistent, machine-
readable format and updated promptly so providers and technology partners can implement 
these requirements in a practical and scalable way. 
While hospitals appreciate the direction of the proposed rule, we urge CMS to recognize that 
streamlining prior authorization does not by itself resolve the underlying overuse of prior 
authorization requirements. We continue to have concerns about the breadth of services and 
drugs subject to prior authorization, repeated approvals for ongoing therapy, benefit design 
complexity and payor practices that shift administrative burden to providers without adding 
value for patients. We encourage CMS to use the data produced by these proposals to identify 
excessive or inappropriate prior authorization use and to consider future policy options that 
limit unnecessary prior authorization for clinically established, evidence-based or continuing 
treatment.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** New Hampshire Hospital Association (NHHA); signed by Steve Ahnen, President.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / healthcare provider association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** NHHA represents New Hampshire hospitals and health systems. The letter identifies Christian Ramsey, Director of Financial Policy & Reimbursement, as the contact.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

NHHA strongly supports CMS’s proposals to expand electronic prior authorization for drugs, improve denial communications, align decision timeframes, and increase transparency, particularly for hospital-administered medical benefit drugs. It urges CMS to strengthen denial specificity, require meaningful reporting and usability, pair technical standards with operational oversight, and ensure payer APIs reduce manual workarounds rather than merely achieving nominal conformance.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL/RFI direct data entry and workflow concerns.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; reference to the 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule. Specific CFR citations are not central to the comment.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR-based APIs; NCPDP standards; implementation guides; API endpoint reporting; usage metrics; prior authorization API; EHR/vendor workflows; conformance testing.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extend ePA requirements to drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** Hospitals face delays for physician-administered drugs, infusion therapies, oncology treatments, specialty pharmaceuticals, and other medically necessary services. Manual portals, faxes, phone calls, and duplicative documentation divert clinical staff from patient care.
- **Specific request:** Finalize ePA requirements for drugs and ensure implementation aligns with clinical workflows, especially for complex and time-sensitive medical benefit therapies.

**Topic 2: Specific denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with stronger standard.
- **Rationale:** Vague denials such as “not medically necessary” do not identify coverage criteria, missing documentation, or clinical reasons, preventing efficient correction, appeal, or patient counseling.
- **Specific request:** Require denial notices to identify the basis for the decision, missing documentation or clinical information, and steps needed for resubmission or appeal.

**Topic 3: Decision timeframes and continuity of care**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with future strengthening.
- **Rationale:** Consistent response expectations reduce administrative burden, but urgent therapies and stable ongoing regimens may need shorter turnaround and protection from repeated reauthorization disruptions.
- **Specific request:** Continue exploring shorter timeframes for clinically urgent therapies and for ongoing treatment where patients are stable.

**Topic 4: Prior authorization metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support with more granular reporting.
- **Rationale:** Numeric counts and public metrics can reveal payers creating unnecessary barriers, but aggregate reporting can obscure delays and denials.
- **Specific request:** Require consistent definitions, easy-to-find public posting, distinctions between standard/expedited requests, initial denials, appeals, extended reviews, and eventually service-level or drug-level reporting. Consider a centralized CMS platform.

**Topic 5: API endpoint reporting and usability oversight**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support with operational safeguards.
- **Rationale:** Consistent technical requirements can reduce custom interfaces, but payers may technically comply while maintaining burdensome workflows or incomplete data exchange.
- **Specific request:** Pair technical standards with oversight of API functionality, reliability, testing, fallback expectations, provider-facing usability, transparency into testing results, and clear distinction between technical conformance and operational usability.

**Topic 6: Standards transitions and HIPAA modernization**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support with staged implementation.
- **Rationale:** Standards modernization can support administrative simplification, but transitions must avoid disruption and protect provider workflows.
- **Specific request:** Coordinate CMS/ONC timelines, conformance expectations, and version transitions; ensure standards are mature, tested, and usable at scale.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1-S3, S18, S32, S37 (FHIR IGs and implementation):** NHHA supports updated FHIR-based standards and required implementation guides but asks CMS to require robust conformance testing, practical usability, and fallback processes.
- **S12, S15, S21, S28 (medical benefit drugs):** NHHA strongly supports including medical benefit drugs, especially chemotherapy, immunotherapy, biologics, infusions, and provider-administered specialty drugs.
- **S14, S19, S22, S25, S31 (pharmacy benefit drugs):** NHHA supports automated exchanges for pharmacy benefits but focuses more heavily on medical benefit drug workflows.
- **S16-S17 (denial reasons):** Strong response; require specific denial rationales with missing information and appeal/resubmission steps.
- **S20, S43 (timeframes):** Supports alignment and shortening while encouraging future reductions for urgent and continuing therapies.
- **S23-S24, S26-S27, S33 (API endpoint reporting):** Supports payer endpoint reporting and standardized publication.
- **S29-S30, S34-S35 (metrics):** Supports expanded PA metrics and requests more granularity, consistency, public accessibility, and centralized reporting.
- **S44-S56 (HIPAA PA standards):** Supports modernization if phased and operationally practical.
- **S60-S65 (ONC updates):** Supports updated standards with coordinated transitions and attention to implementation readiness.
- **Other solicitations:** State extension, FF-SHOP exceptions, Open Payments CMP, and lab/DMEPOS RFIs are not central to this comment.

## 6. THEMES

- PROVIDER-BURDEN
- PATIENT-ACCESS
- EXISTING-WORKFLOWS
- TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY
- TRANSPARENCY
- STANDARDS-MATURITY
- API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- API-USAGE-METRICS
- VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM
- IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE

## 7. POTENTIAL CMS ACTION ITEMS

1. Finalize drug ePA requirements with hospital workflow-specific implementation guidance.
2. Define a stronger denial specificity standard.
3. Require drug- or service-level PA metrics and make reporting easier to locate and compare.
4. Require conformance testing, public testing transparency, and provider-facing usability validation for payer APIs.
5. Establish fallback expectations for API failures.
6. Coordinate standards version transitions across CMS, ONC, payers, EHR vendors, and intermediaries.

## 8. NOTABLE QUOTES / EVIDENCE

- NHHA cites AMA survey findings that 95% of physicians reported PA delays necessary care and 79% said PA can lead to treatment abandonment.
- NHHA emphasizes that APIs that technically meet a standard but do not return actionable information or reduce manual workarounds will not achieve the rule’s goals.

## 9. OVERALL ASSESSMENT

NHHA is a provider-association support-with-modifications comment. Its strongest value is operational: denial specificity, medical benefit drug workflows, real-world usability, conformance testing, reporting granularity, and safeguards against nominal API compliance.
